summary.title: The Plumber's Approach to Distributed Systems
summary.one_liner: Learn how to route each request to a single instance that owns a business-domain partition (such as a customer), so its in-memory state can be handled single-threaded for lower latency and fewer correctness problems than stateless microservices.
keywords: how to avoid race conditions without locks
when not to use stateful design
takeaways: Partition work by a business domain (e.g., customer) so one instance exclusively handles all requests for each unit, avoiding contention resolved only via database transactions.

Use a routing table (ideally a compact interval map) held in memory by each instance, kept in sync by a coordination service such as etcd, with exclusive, long-lived ownership enforced by leases or locks.
Run one lightweight handler per domain unit that processes requests sequentially, which makes caching and atomicity simpler, and allows periodic or timer-driven actions.
The in-memory state is not durable: writes must still reach the database, and ownership changes or crashes lose handler state.
The approach suits low-latency systems with substantial in-memory state; if a stateless design works well, it is simpler and preferable.
summary.summary: The article argues that many distributed systems built as request-driven stateless microservices sacrifice correctness and latency at scale. It proposes a "plumber's approach" where each request is routed to one instance that owns a partition of a business domain, such as customers, and that instance processes that partition's requests in a single-threaded handler. It uses a pizza-ordering example to walk through choosing a partition key, routing via DNS, hardcoded config, or a coordination service, and dispatching to per-customer handlers. The post closes with the tradeoffs: in-memory state is not the durable source of truth, partitioning fits some domains better than others, and blocking or slow I/O can limit handler scope.
